proposals.claim: The increase in timeouts from 2 of 40 to 11 of 40 is caused by the increase in parallelism from 1 to 8 under the new scheduler, not by the scheduler change itself.
proposals.falsifier: Run the same 40-operation workload with the new scheduler at 1, 2, 4, and 8 concurrent requests under identical load and provider limits; if the timeout rate does not increase monotonically with the concurrency ceiling, the causal role of parallelism from 1 to 8 is not supported.
proposals.why_plausible: Raising concurrency from 1 to 8 while using the same underlying provider could exceed rate/capacity limits, and the observed timeout count rose in direct proportion to the parallelism change. The user's own evidence note and the correlated timing pattern make concurrency exhaustion a plausible causal pathway.
required_evidence: Timeouts measured per concurrency level (1, 2, 4, 8) under the new scheduler
Identical workload composition and request size distribution at each concurrency level
Provider rate-limit and quota status recorded during each concurrency level
competing_explanations: Rate-limit or quota exhaustion independent of parallelism
Larger or batchier request sizes introduced after the scheduler change
Transient infrastructure degradation or retry behaviour unrelated to concurrency

proposals.claim: The higher timeout count is driven by provider-side rate limiting or quota exhaustion triggered by the scheduler switch, independent of the parallelism change.
proposals.falsifier: Measure provider rate-limit headers, quota consumption, and error codes for each of the 40 operations; if timeout occurrences are concentrated in distinct rate-limit windows or correlate with quota spikes rather than concurrency levels, the scheduler switch is not established as the cause.
proposals.why_plausible: The evidence explicitly notes that provider limits and request-size distribution were not checked, and a parallel ramp from 1 to 8 can easily push total requests per second past a provider threshold. If provider limits are the binding constraint, the concurrency increase is a confounder rather than the cause.
required_evidence: Provider rate-limit headers captured per request
Provider quota/consumption metrics at each concurrency level
Error-type breakdown (timeout vs throttling vs server error) per operation
competing_explanations: Larger request sizes after the scheduler change
Transient infrastructure degradation or retry behaviour

proposals.claim: The hypothesis that the scheduler change caused the timeout increase is unproven; the observed correlation between the scheduler change and higher timeouts is confounded by unmeasured provider limits, request-size distribution, and load differences.
assumptions: The 40-operation samples are comparable in workload and request size
No other configuration differences were introduced at the same time as the scheduler change and concurrency increase
Timeout events are attributable to the same underlying failure mode

proposals.claim: The true causal factor behind the increase in timeouts from 2 of 40 to 11 of 40 between the old and new scheduling configurations
proposals.why_unknown: The evidence packet explicitly flags that identical-load comparisons are absent, provider limits and request-size distribution were not checked, and the currentness of the evidence cannot be determined. Therefore the causal role of the scheduler change and the role of parallelism remain open questions.
required_evidence: A/B comparison of the old and new scheduler at identical load and request-size distribution
Per-operation timeout classification and provider limit metrics
A controlled concurrency ramp experiment with the new scheduler
Replication of the original 40-operation workload under both configurations

proposals.claim: In the Birch lab control experiment using the old scheduler with 1 parallel request, 2 out of 40 operations timed out.
After switching to the new scheduler and increasing parallelism to 8, 11 out of 40 operations timed out.
The combined change of scheduler and increase in parallelism from 1 to 8 was associated with an increase in timeout rate from 5% to 27.5%.
assumptions: The two experimental runs are comparable despite different parallelism levels.
The observed difference in timeout rates is not due to random variation.

proposals.claim: The new scheduler causes higher timeout rates under high parallelism due to resource contention, rather than the parallelism increase alone.
proposals.falsifier: A controlled experiment where the scheduler is changed while keeping parallelism constant at 8; if timeout rate does not increase compared to old scheduler, the hypothesis is falsified.
proposals.why_plausible: The experiment changed both scheduler and parallelism simultaneously, making it impossible to isolate effects; however, the new scheduler may have different concurrency handling that amplifies timeouts when many requests are processed in parallel.
required_evidence: Run old scheduler at parallelism 8 and measure timeout rate.
Run new scheduler at parallelism 1 and measure timeout rate.
Collect provider limit metrics and request size distributions for both conditions.
competing_explanations: The increase in timeouts is solely due to higher parallelism, independent of scheduler.
Provider rate limits were reached under higher parallelism causing timeouts.
The distribution of request sizes changed between experiments, leading to more timeouts.

proposals.claim: The precise cause of the increased timeout rate in the Birch lab experiment remains unknown.
proposals.why_unknown: The experiment changed two variables (scheduler and parallelism) simultaneously, and provider limits and request size distributions were not controlled or measured.
required_evidence: Controlled experiments varying scheduler and parallelism independently.
Data on provider limits and request sizes under both conditions.
